title: Space Startups Raise Record $20.8 Billion as Infrastructure Bets Surge
excerpt: Seraphim's third-quarter report shows funding nearly tripled from the prior quarter across a record 216 deals, led by launch and space-access companies.
body:
• Space startups raised a record $20.8 billion in the third quarter, nearly triple the $7.4 billion raised in the second quarter, according to Seraphim.
  • Even excluding Blue Origin's $10 billion financing, investment hit an all-time high of $10.8 billion across a record 216 deals.
  • Launch and space-access companies took $16.4 billion across 120 deals; space services such as satellite communications and Earth observation raised $4 billion.
  • North America accounted for about 70% of global funding year-to-date, while China posted a quarterly high of $3.3 billion across 49 deals.

Space startups attracted a record $20.8 billion in funding in the third quarter, as investors poured money into launch providers, manufacturing and other infrastructure ventures, according to a report by global investment firm Seraphim cited by Reuters and carried by The Economic Times.

The total was nearly triple the $7.4 billion invested in the second quarter and more than double the previous peak. One deal dominates the headline number: Blue Origin's $10 billion financing. Strip it out, and the quarter still set an all-time high at $10.8 billion — the detail that makes the record more than a single-company story.

Infrastructure takes the money

Deal volume rose with deal value. Seraphim counted a record 216 completed deals in the quarter, up from 140 in the previous three months. Infrastructure-related businesses accounted for the bulk of the activity: companies in launch and broader space access attracted $16.4 billion across 120 deals, while satellite communications, Earth observation and other space-service companies raised $4 billion.

https://x.com/businessline/status/2110307640316395967

The quarter's largest rounds named in the report included $1.37 billion for Hadrian, $1 billion for Stoke Space and $500 million for K2 Space. Seraphim linked the fundraising to a growing pipeline of commercial orders and government-backed programmes, even as SpaceX remains the industry's dominant force.

"Capital is following evidence of commercial and institutional demand, not just residual IPO enthusiasm."

— Lucas Bishop, Vice President, Seraphim Space

Defence demand and a geographic split

Seraphim's Lucas Bishop said defence and sovereign demand are increasingly supporting investment in launch, manufacturing and orbital infrastructure, as governments prioritise domestic space capabilities. That shifts the sector's funding base from consumer-style enthusiasm towards state-backed, multi-year demand.

Geography remains concentrated. North America accounted for about 70% of global funding year-to-date. China, however, recorded a quarterly high of $3.3 billion across 49 deals, underlining that the infrastructure race is not a one-country story.

The listed-company contrast

The private surge contrasts with weaker performance among listed space companies. Bishop noted that many publicly traded space firms remain loss-making, and that SpaceX's scale and visibility may have drawn investor attention away from smaller listed peers.

Seraphim expects funding to moderate from the third quarter's exceptional level, but to stay above historical norms as more companies enter growth and scale-up phases. For engineers and founders in the Indian diaspora working in aerospace hubs from Los Angeles to Bengaluru, the practical read is that capital is available — but it is flowing to infrastructure with demonstrable commercial or government demand, not to concepts alone.
